Abstract: Developing efficient catalysts for steering electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction 1 (CO2RR) toward high-value chemicals beyond CO and formic acid is highly desirable. 2 Herein, we have developed copper-based catalysts confined within a rationally designed 3 covalent triazine framework (CTF-B), featuring a CuN2Cl2 structure, for selective CO2RR to 4 hydrocarbons with a maximal Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 81.3% and a FE of C2H4 up to 5 30.6%. Operando X-ray adsorption fine structure analyses reveal the potential-driven 6 dynamic formation of Cu atomic clusters, together with the time-dependent and Cu 7 content-dependent CO2RR performance associated with the catalyst activation, definitely 8 uncovering that the aggregated Cu clusters confined within CTF-B are the active sites. 9 Further probing experiment of CO electroreduction not only verifies that CO is one of the key 10 intermediates for CO2RR but also demonstrates the improved selectivity to C2 chemicals, 11 with a maximal FE of 68.4% (C2H4: 35.0% and acetate: 33.4%), possibly originating from the 12 accelerative C-C coupling reaction due to the increased CO coverage and enhancive local pH 13 in CO-saturated electrolyte. Interestingly, acetate is identified as the only liquid product, 14 mostly likely benefiting from the dominated low-coordination active sites of confined Cu 15 aggregation and favorable chemical confinement environment of CTF-B. The strategy of 16 constructing efficient metallo-electrocatalysts by means of the confinement in covalent 17 organic framework along with operando identification of active sites sheds light on the 18 rational catalyst design and structure-property relationship. 19
Keywords: electrochemical CO2 reduction, operando characterization, covalent triazine 20 framework, confined Cu catalysts, CO electroreduction, hydrocarbon, acetate21

sections.heading: 1. INTRODUCTION 1
sections.text:
The electrochemical reduction of CO2 to high-value chemicals powered by renewable and 2 excess electricity has emerged as a promising approach to implement the energy conversion 3 and storage.1-3 To date, plenty of materials have been demonstrated as efficient catalysts for 4 the production of CO and formic acid from electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction 5 (CO2RR),4-10 but it still remains a big challenge for CO2RR to multi-electron products, such 6 as hydrocarbons and multi-carbon oxygenated chemicals.11-14 Among metal catalysts, copper 7 (Cu) based materials have been demonstrated as the only efficient electrocatalysts for deep 8 catalytic reduction of CO2.15-20 Nevertheless, inorganic Cu compounds usually suffer from 9 low selectivity and insufficient stability for CO2RR due to the competitive hydrogen 10 evolution reaction (HER) and the irreversible structural transformation.21-23 Therefore, 11 searching for the novel strategy for the rational catalyst design and gaining new insight into 12 structure-property relationship for CO2RR are highly desirable. 13
Covalent organic frameworks (COFs), especially covalent triazine frameworks (CTFs) 14 with the adjustable building blocks, rationally designed ligand units and superior chemical 15 stability, are identified as robust platforms to prepare well-defined catalysts by precisely 16 anchoring metal ions.24-26 At present, CTF anchored metals have been applied to many 17 electrocatalytic reactions, such as oxygen reduction reaction,27 hydrogen oxidation reaction28 18 and CO2RR.29, 30 Although the metal sites (nickel, cobalt, etc.) anchored on CTF only 19 exhibited the CO2RR selectivity toward two-electron products, the advantage in term of 20 activity and selectivity over molecular catalysts was observed.29 Theoretically, CTF featured 21 with the rationally designed organic ligands and porous framework structures might offer the 22 unique chemical environment for confining and stabilizing active metal species, consequently 23 promoting the formation of the desirable products.24, 26 Thus, it might be a novel strategy to 24

tailor Cu catalysts for CO2RR to value-added chemicals by taking advantage of the tunable 1 chemical and spatial confined environments of porous organic framework. To the best of our 2 knowledge, reports related to the rationally designed Cu catalysts confined in CTFs or other 3 COF materials for efficient CO2RR are rare. 4
Electrocatalytic CO2 reduction reaction normally occurs at large overpotentials, where the 5 most of catalysts prefer to self-reconstruction.22, 31-34 Although the active sites were often 6 identified from the post-electrolysis catalysts, sometimes it would lead to imprecise or even 7 misleading conclusion regarding the structure-property relationship because the true active 8 sites under applied potentials might be different.31, 32, 35 For example, Weng et al. reported that 9 the commercial Cu phthalocyanine underwent the structural change to form Cu clusters at the 10 working potential of CO2RR.31 The reconstruction of Cu sites was also observed on a Cu/N 11 co-doped carbon material by operando X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS).32 Both of the 12 operando measurements affirmed that the in situ-formed Cu aggregation rather than 13 single-atom sites before and after reaction should be responsible for CO2RR toward 14 multi-electron chemicals although the decided conclusion about active sites failed to be 15 drawn due to the coexistence of Cu aggregation and single-atom sites under the reaction 16 conditions.31, 32 Undoubtedly, it is still extremely important to employ operando structural 17 identification for the accurate understanding of the correlation between the catalytic behavior 18 and active sites.36, 37 19
Herein, a newly designed CTF with the bipyridine unit was prepared as the well-defined 20 platform for confining Cu sites, which would enable us to diagnose the active site during 21 CO2RR. Both aberration-corrected high-angle annular dark-field scanning transmission 22 electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) and XAS measurements confirm that Cu exists in the 23 form of single-atom state within the prepared complex (CTF-Cu), featured with its initial 24

CuN2Cl2 structure. Such a CTF-Cu material exhibits a maximal Faradaic efficiency (FE) of 1 81.3% for producing hydrocarbons during CO2RR. Operando X-ray absorption fine structure 2 (XAFS) analyses reveal the potential-driven dynamic formation of Cu atomic clusters 3 (Cu-ACs), along with the time-dependent and Cu content-dependent CO2RR performance 4 associated with the catalyst activation, definitely confirming that in situ-formed Cu-ACs are 5 the active sites of CO2RR. Further probing experiment of CO electroreduction not only 6 verifies that CO is one of the key intermediates during CO2RR but also demonstrates the 7 notably improved C2 products selectivity and the exclusive formation of acetate in liquid 8 products. The strategy of constructing confined Cu catalysts within CTF together with 9 operando identification of active sites paves the way for the rational catalyst design and for 10 the structure-property investigation for highly efficient CO2RR. 11

sections.heading: 2. RESULTS AND DISCUSSION 12
sections.text:
2.1. Synthesis and Characterization of CTFs and CTF-Cu. The CTFs were prepared 13 using an in situ oxidation method.38 As shown in Figure 1a, [1, 1’-biphenyl]-4, 4’-bis 14 (carboximidamide) (PCM) and [2, 2’- bipyridine]-5, 5’-dimethanol (BPM) were used as the 15 unit blocks with a molar ratio of 2/1 for preparing the CTF with the bipyridine unit (CTF-B). 16 For a comparison, the CTF without the bipyridine unit was also prepared (CTF-R, Supporting 17 Information for detailed procedure). The formation of triazine rings can be verified by 18 Fourier-transformed infrared (FTIR) spectra (Figure S3), in which two characteristic 19 absorption bands at 1373 and 1508 cm−1 indicate the aromatic C−N stretching and breathing 20 vibration of the triazine unit, respectively.38, 39 Powder X-ray diffraction (PXRD) patterns 21 (Figure 1b and Figure S4) of the CTFs show certain intensive peaks, revealing that the 22 as-prepared CTFs exhibit good crystallinity.40 CTF-B exhibits five features at approximately 23 4.7°, 8.3°, 13.2°, 18.1° and 25.1° (Figure 1b). However, the PXRD is hard to match with a 24

Nitrogen sorption experiments indicate that CTF-B has a surface area of 488 m2 2 g−1 with a total pore volume of 0.28 cm3 g−1. From the pore distribution (Figure 1c), it can be 3 found that two kinds of pores width (12.6 Å and 21.6 Å) exist within CTF-B, which are close 4 to the theoretical value of the pore of AB and AA staking model respectively. The result is in 5 agreement with the PXRD result that CTF-B is a mixture of AA and AB stacking. 6

2.3. Operando Diagnosis of Active Sites. We further conducted operando XAS 10 measurements on CTF-Cu-4.8% during CO2RR to reveal the activation process. Figures 5a-c 11 show the time-dependent XAFS spectra collected at –1.45 V vs. SHE. From the XANES 12 spectra and their corresponding derivative curves, Cu(II) species began to be reduced to Cu(0) 13 state according to the negative shift of the Cu K-edge position, the attenuated intensity of 14 white line peak (indicated in Figure 5a)43 and the emerging Cu(0) peak (indicated in Figure 15 5b) after 20 min. At the same time, the Cu-Cu bond peak is formed according to the 16 Fourier-transformed EXAFS spectra (Figure 5c). Apparently, the reduced Cu atoms within 17 CTF-Cu aggregate to form Cu clusters or nanoparticles. With an increase in electrolysis time, 18 the intensity of the peak at 1.5–1.6 Å, associated with single-atom sites, presents a decrease 19 tendency as a whole. Meanwhile, the intensity of Cu-Cu bond peak at ca. 2.2 Å increases 20 gradually and then reaches the relatively stable level but far lower than that of Cu foil, 21 strongly suggesting the formation of Cu-ACs within the CTF-Cu during the electrolysis.31, 32 22 Thus, the dynamic formation of Cu-ACs should be responsible for the activation process and 23 namely Cu-ACs are the active sites for CO2RR. 24

2.4. The Investigation of Redox Behavior. The XAFS spectra collected at some different 7 tested potentials after one-hour electrolysis on CTF-Cu-4.8% are displayed in Figure S25. 8 According to the XANES (Figure S25a) and Fourier-transformed EXAFS spectra (Figure 9 S25b), partial Cu(II) sites have been reduced to Cu(0) state and aggregate together at –0.5 V 10 vs. SHE on CTF-Cu-4.8%. Obviously, Cu sites aggregate more easily at more negative 11 potential. Additionally, we performed the cyclic voltammetry (CV) tests with the changed 12 negative potential and the constant positive potential (0.4 V vs. SHE) to further investigate 13 the redox behavior of CTF-Cu-4.8% (Figure S26). When the negative potential shifts to –0.2 14 V vs. SHE, a pair of oxidation peaks emerge and the intensity increases with the more 15 negative potential. Considering the potential-dependent formation of Cu aggregation 16 uncovered by the operando XAFS spectra (Figure S25), it can be deduced that the oxidation 17 peaks originate from the oxidation of Cu aggregation. The oxidation peak around 0.08 V vs. 18 SHE could be attributed to the oxidation of Cu aggregation to Cu(I) species and the peak 19 around 0.22 V vs. SHE could be attributed to the subsequent oxidation of Cu(I) species to 20 Cu(II) species. Correspondingly, partial Cu(II) sites within CTF-Cu-4.8% could be reduced to 21 Cu(0) state at –0.2 V vs. SHE although the CV curve displays no reduction peak and only 22 increased current at more negative potential. We have also performed the CV scan over the 23 potential range of –0.4 ~ 0.4 V vs. SHE on the sample after one-hour reaction at –1.5 V vs. 24 SHE. As shown in Figure S27, only an evident oxidation peak at 0.13 V is observed, probably 25

Intrigued by the absence of Cu aggregation from the ex-situ XAFS spectra, the possible 12 structural transformation of Cu-ACs under different conditions was further investigated by 13 XAS measurements. Firstly, it is demonstrated that the formed Cu-ACs at –1.5 V vs. SHE are 14 still retained in CO2-saturated electrolyte after reaction (Figures S30–S31). After applying a 15 potential of 0.2 V vs. SHE on the sample with formed Cu-ACs in CO2-saturated electrolyte, 16 operando XAFS analyses show the disappearance of metallic copper phase and no 17 characteristic peaks attributed to CuO or Cu2O (Figures S30–S31). ICP-OES measurements 18 confirmed the absence of dissolved Cu ions in the electrolyte, again inferring that most of the 19 stripped Cu ions could be anchored by CTF-B might due to the strong Cu-bipyridine 20 coordination. Additionally, the XAFS spectra of the post-electrolysis sample in air-accessible 21 electrolyte also indicate the disaggregation of Cu-ACs (Figures S30–S31). Therefore, it can 22 be concluded that the structural transformation from Cu-ACs to Cu single-atom state can be 23 driven by either suitable oxidation potential or oxidizing atmosphere. 24

2.5. CO Probing Experiment. Further CO electroreduction as probing experiment was 1 conducted to explore the possible formation mechanism of multi-electron products. It is 2 worth noting that the activation behavior of CTF-Cu catalysts during the reaction is also 3 observed (Figure 6a), probably indicative of the potential-driven formation of Cu aggregation 4 as active sites. Figure 6b displays FEs of electrocatalytic CO reduction at –1.5 V vs. SHE on 5 CTF-Cu catalysts. CH4, C2H4 and acetate are the main products, strongly indicating that CO 6 is a key reaction intermediate for these products during CO2RR. Interestingly, a strikingly 7 increased selectivity for producing C2 chemicals is observed during CO reduction compared 8 with CO2RR, possibly originating from the accelerative C-C coupling reaction due to the 9 increased CO coverage and enhancive local pH around catalytic sites in CO-saturated 10 electrolyte.50-55 The maximal FE of 68.4% for producing C2 chemicals, with the FE of C2H4 11 and acetate reaching 35.0% and 33.4% respectively, is achieved at –1.5 V vs. SHE on 12 CTF-Cu-4.8% (Figure 6b and Figure S32). Importantly, the exclusive formation of acetate in 13 liquid products (Figure S33) definitely manifests the advantage of CTF-Cu, which would be 14 utilized as a catalytic platform for carefully investigating the mechanism and 15 structure-property relationship of acetate production by the combination of in-situ 16 high-resolution TEM, for direct visualization of the Cu aggregation to obtain the detailed size 17 and dominated crystal face during the reaction, with further theoretical calculation. The 18 excellent acetate selectivity might be attributable to the abundant low-coordination active 19 sites of confined Cu aggregation and to the favorable chemical confinement environment of 20 CTF-B. 21

sections.heading: 3. CONCLUSIONS 4
sections.text:
CTF-B confined Cu catalysts were constructed for selective and robust CO2RR to 5 hydrocarbons with the maximal FE up to 81.3%. Operando XAFS analyses reveal the 6 potential-driven dynamic formation of Cu-ACs, in combination with the Cu 7 content-dependent activation process, evidencing that Cu-ACs stabilized by CTF-B are the 8 active sites for CO2RR. CO probing experiment discloses that CO is one of the main 9 intermediates during CO2RR, clearly demonstrating that direct electroreduction of CO instead 10 of CO2 not only significantly improves the selectivity for producing C2 products but also 11 steers the exclusive formation of acetate in liquid products, which could be attributed to the 12 synergistic effect of the dominated low-coordination active sites of confined Cu aggregation 13 and the favorable chemical confinement environment of CTF-B. Our findings definitely 14 demonstrate the novel strategy of combining the CTF confinement with operando 15 characterization for the rational design of the metallo-electrocatalysts and the 16 structure-property investigation of efficient CO2RR.17
